children.text: kaumārye paṭhyatāṃ vidyā śaitye saṃpālyatāṃ ca gauḥ /
children.translated_text: In youth let learning be pursued, in the cold season let the cow be tended,

children.text: kṣettraṃ ca karṣyatāṃ pītaṃ trayaḥ suphalahetavaḥ // 1 //
children.translated_text: and let the field be plowed when moist — these three are the causes of good fruit. [1]

children.text: gate 'pi vayasi grāhyā vidyā sarvātmanā budhaiḥ /
children.translated_text: Even when youth has passed, learning should be grasped wholeheartedly by the wise,
for even if it may not bear fruit [in this life], it is not easily obtained in another birth. [2]
Let effort be made in [acquiring] virtues — what is the use of ostentation?
Cows devoid of milk are not sold by [the ringing of] bells. [3]

children.text: guṇini guṇajño ramate nāguṇaśīlasya guṇini paritoṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: One who knows virtue delights in the virtuous; there is no satisfaction of the virtue-less person in one who is virtuous —
The bee goes from the forest to the lotus, but not the frog, even though it dwells there. [4]

body.translated_text: Among the virtuous, wealthy persons are rare; and among the wealthy, virtuous persons are likewise [rare]. [5]

children.translated_text: Many are the regions of the earth, but those containing gems are rare;
Rare among living beings are those endowed with [good] mother and father. [6]

children.text: guṇāḥ kurvanti dūtatvaṃ dūre 'pi basatāṃ satām /
children.translated_text: Virtues serve as messengers for the good, even when they dwell far away;
To smell the fragrance of the <s>ketakī</s> flower, the bees come of their own accord. [7]

children.text: vidvatvaṃ ca nṛpatvaṃ ca naiva tulyaṃ kadācana /
children.translated_text: Scholarship and kingship are never equal;

children.text: svadeśe pūjyate rājā vidvān sarvatra pūjyate // 8 //
children.translated_text: A king is honored in his own country, but a scholar is honored everywhere. [8]

children.text: alpastu kālo vividhāśca vidhā ḥ simāyuṣo yā kiyatī? na buddhā /
children.translated_text: Time is short and the branches of knowledge are manifold — of one whose life is limited, how much is understood?

children.text: haṃsā labhante ca yathā payo 'dbhyas tathaiva tatvaṃ labhatāṃ ca yattat // 9 //
children.translated_text: Just as swans obtain milk from water, so let one extract the essence from that [ocean of knowledge]. [9]
Those dwelling in one place, after a very long time, must indeed be separated;

children.text: vicchedānna hi cāntaraṃ kimapi tat tyājyaṃ na kiṃ tatsthalam /
children.translated_text: Since there is no gap from separation, should that place then not be abandoned?

children.text: vaivaśyāddhi viyogato manasi jāyante vidhātā ati
children.translated_text: For when separation occurs through force of circumstance, great sorrows arise in the mind;

children.text: tatsthānaṃ yadi hīyate sahajataḥ syāccātiśāntiḥ sukham // 10 //
children.translated_text: If one relinquishes that place [voluntarily], there would be exceedingly great peace and happiness. [10]
Even for those living together, with the wicked there is non-attachment, like the lotus and water;
Even for the good dwelling far away, there is affection, like the night-lily and the moon. [11]

children.text: prapañcā yatnaoto heyāḥ saṃsargaḥ kriyatāṃ satām /
children.translated_text: Worldly entanglements should be avoided with effort; let association be made with the virtuous;
A single day freed from the fear of disease is better than a hundred years [without such freedom]. [12]
All worldly endeavors should be abandoned; if this is impossible, then
one should become oriented toward the attainment of <s>nirvāṇa</s> (liberation) — this is its remedy. [13]

body.text: udayantvamūni subahūni mahāmahāṃsi cando cando 'pyalaṃ bhuvanamaṇḍalamaṇḍanāya / sūryādūte na tadudeti na cāstameti yenoditena dinamastamitena rātriḥ // 14 //
body.translated_text: Let these many great luminaries — moon after moon — rise, each sufficient to adorn the circle of the world; yet without the sun, none of them truly rises nor sets — he by whose rising there is day, and by whose setting there is night. [14]

children.text: yadudeti vinā sūrya tejasvi tanna jāyate /
children.translated_text: Whatever rises without the sun, that does not become radiant;
Better is the rising of the sun — what use is the rising of others? [15]

children.text: mūdhni vā sarvalokasya śīryate vana eva vā // 16 /
children.translated_text: either upon the head of all the world, or withering in the forest itself. [16]

children.text: vāṇi kaṭhorā bhaṇitā hi duṣṭairyā sarparūpā sujanān hinasti /
children.translated_text: Harsh speech uttered by the wicked, which like a serpent harms the good —

children.text: te bheṣajaṃ kṣāntimayaṃ ca prajñāṃ saṃsevya cintārahitā bhavanti // 17 //
children.translated_text: they, resorting to patience as medicine and wisdom, become free from worry. [17]

body.translated_text: Like a cluster of flowers, there are but two destinies for the great-souled:

children.translated_text: The steadfast, even when afflicted by hardship, do not become despondent;

children.text: praviśya vadanaṃ rāhoḥ kiṃ nodeti punaḥ śaśī // 18 //
children.translated_text: Having entered the mouth of <s>Rāhu</s>, does the moon not rise again? [18]
He whose mind has melted with compassion for all beings —
what need has he of knowledge, liberation, matted locks, ashes, or robes? [19]

children.text: vanāni dahato vahneḥ sakhā bhavati mārutaḥ /
children.translated_text: The wind becomes the friend of the fire that burns forests;

children.text: sa eva dīpanāśāya kṛśe kasyāsti sauhṛdam // 20 //
children.translated_text: that same [wind] destroys a lamp — who is a friend to the weak? [20]
He who is without virtues becomes virtuous through virtues praised by others;
even <s>Indra</s> is diminished by virtues proclaimed by himself. [21]
One of noble family may be arrogant; a wealthy person may be coupled with miserliness;
the gods condemn such ones — this creation is like water and fire [incompatible]. [22]

children.text: dūrastho 'pi samīpastho yo yasya manasi sthitaḥ /
children.translated_text: Though far away, he is near who is established in one's mind;
though nearby, he who is not in one's heart is far away. [23]

children.text: pareṣāṃ vaibhavaṃ dṛṣṭvā mano yasya prakupyati /
children.translated_text: He whose mind becomes agitated upon seeing the prosperity of others —

children.text: na tasyārthopalabdhistu citaṃ puṇyaṃ ca naśyati // 24 //
children.translated_text: for him there is no acquisition of wealth, and accumulated merit perishes. [24]

children.text: rāgopamaṃ nāsti malaṃ hi loke īrṣyopamā nāsti ca kāpi hāniḥ /
children.translated_text: There is no impurity in the world equal to passion; no loss comparable to envy;

children.text: yāñcāsamo nāsti ca ko 'pi bandhurdānopamo nāsti ca mitravargaḥ // 25 //
children.translated_text: no bondage comparable to begging; and no company of friends comparable to generosity. [25]

children.text: kṣudhāsamā nāsti śarīravedanā cintāsamā nāsti śarīraśoṣaṇā /
children.translated_text: There is no bodily suffering equal to hunger; no bodily wasting equal to worry;

children.text: guṇaiḥ samā nāsti śarīrabhūṣaṇā kṣāntyā samaṃ nāsti śarīravarmaṃ vai // 26 //
children.translated_text: no bodily ornament equal to virtues; and no bodily armor equal to patience. [26]

children.text: dhanena kiṃ kṣudrajanasya mitraiḥ kiṃ vañcakasyāpi ca matsarasya /
children.translated_text: What use is wealth to a mean person? What use are friends to a deceitful and envious one?

children.text: kiṃ hānidasyātiguṇagrahaiśca kiṃ vā vipattau vimukhātmajena // 27 //
children.translated_text: What use is the seizing of great virtues to one inclined to loss? And what use is offspring who turns away in adversity? [27]

children.text: sarvathā svahitamācaraṇīyaṃ kiṃ kariṣyati jano bahujalpaḥ /
children.translated_text: By all means, one should practice what is beneficial to oneself — what will people with their much chatter accomplish?

children.text: bidyate hi na sa kaścidupāyaḥ sarvalokaparitoṣakaro yaḥ // 28 //
children.translated_text: For there exists no such means that pleases the entire world. [28]

children.text: prasaṅgasyānukūlo yaḥ prajña eva sa pālayet /
children.translated_text: He who is favorable to the occasion — let the wise person indeed protect him;

children.text: satyāsatye ca maitridveṣau kuryāt svaparaiḥ saha // 29 //
children.translated_text: in truth and untruth, he should exercise friendship and enmity with both self and others. [29]

children.text: na dviṣantaḥ kṣayaṃ yānti yāvajjīvamapi ghnataḥ /
children.translated_text: Enemies do not perish even when one kills throughout an entire lifetime;

children.text: krodhameva tu yo hanti tena sarve dviṣo hatāḥ // 30 //
children.translated_text: but he who slays anger itself — by him all enemies are slain. [30]
Honoring the virtuous is meritorious; the humbling of the wicked [is likewise];
filling the treasury through righteous conduct — better [still] is the examination of the land. [31]
As long as one can see the path, as long as the feet are strong,

children.text: prajñā hrāso na yāvaddhi tāvatkuryāt svayaṃ hitam // 32 //
children.translated_text: as long as wisdom has not declined — so long should one act for one's own welfare. [32]

children.text: vyabhicāreṣvāsattaḥ rājā tasya hi nirakṣaro mantri /
children.translated_text: When the king is attached to misconduct, and his minister is illiterate,

children.text: tadā dhanāśā kutra rakṣyā asavaḥ prayatnena // 33 //
children.translated_text: then where is the hope for wealth? Life should be guarded with effort. [33]
Where everyone is a leader, everyone considers himself a scholar,
everyone desires sovereignty — that assembly comes to ruin. [34]
Let a mouse guard the grain! Let a cat [guard] the butter!

children.text: kākaścālayet pākaṃ vastūnāṃ tatra kā kathā // 35 //
children.translated_text: Let a crow tend the cooking! — what need to speak of [other] matters? [35]
Like a gardener in a garden, not like a charcoal-maker,

children.text: puṣpaṃ puṣpaṃ vicinvīta mūlocchedaṃ na kārayet // 36 //
children.translated_text: one should pick flower after flower, and not cause the uprooting of the roots. [36]

children.text: valmīkaṃ madhujātaṃ ca śuklapakṣe ca candramāḥ /
children.translated_text: An anthill, a honeycomb, and the moon in the bright fortnight,
alms-property and the king's property — [all] increase little by little. [37]

children.text: hīnatā yācane yatra syāttatra na ca yācyatām /
children.translated_text: Where there is degradation in begging, there one should not beg;

children.text: kāmaṃ hi na bhavedindro himājjīvati tittariḥ // 38 //
children.translated_text: even if one may not become <s>Indra</s>, the partridge lives on snow. [38]

children.text: mayūra ! grīṣmasya tu tāpayukta āśāyutaḥ khasya jale bhavestvam /
children.translated_text: O peacock! In the scorching heat of summer, full of hope, you may be [drawn] to the water of the sky;

children.text: kaṇṭhantu no nāmaya gauraveṇa nīre taḍāgasya tu dūṣitasya // 39 //
children.translated_text: but do not bow your neck in reverence to the water of a polluted pond! [39]

body.text:
siṃho balī hariṇaraktapāmāṃsabhojī saṃvatsareṇa kurute ratimekavāram /
yo gardabhaḥ khalu rajaḥkaṇamātrabhojī kāmī bhavedanudinaṃ vada ko 'tra hetuḥ // 40 // sarpāḥ pibanti pavanaṃ na ca durbalāste śuṣkaistṛṇairvanagajā balino bhavanti / kandaiḥ phalairmunivarā gamayanti kālam saṃtoṣa eva puruṣasya paraṃ nidhānam // 41 //
body.translated_text: The lion, powerful, feeding on the flesh and blood of deer, mates but once in a year; yet the donkey, feeding on mere particles of dust, is lustful every day — tell me, what is the reason here? [40] Serpents drink the wind and are not weak; forest elephants become strong on dry grass; the best of sages pass their time on roots and fruits — contentment alone is the supreme treasure of a person. [41]

children.text: sa śobhate puṣpitapuṣpavacca sumaṇḍitaṃ yasya mukhaṃ suvarṇaiḥ /
children.translated_text: He shines like a flowering tree, whose face is well-adorned with [beautiful] words;

children.text: anakṣaraṃ yasya mukhaṃ bhavecvet tannetravaktre bhubi chidravacca // 42 //
children.translated_text: but he whose face is without letters (uneducated) — that is like a hole in the eye and face upon the earth. [42]

children.text: muktāmaṇibhyāṃ ca hi gardabhasya kiṃ śūkarasya priyabhojanena /
children.translated_text: What use are pearls and gems to a donkey? What use is fine food to a pig?

children.text: andhasyadīptyā badhirasya gītaimūrkhasya dharmeṇa kimasti kṛtyam // 43 //
children.translated_text: What use is a lamp to the blind, songs to the deaf, or <s>dharma</s> to a fool? [43]
One who knows only <s>Kātantra</s> grammar, and a physician who knows only <s>Siddhasāra</s>,
and one who bears a wooden sword — all three become objects of ridicule. [44]
'Give' — this word is lowly; 'I shall not give' — even more lowly;
'Take' — this is a noble utterance; 'I shall not take' — most excellent. [45]

children.text: kṣatiṃ bihāya yenāpi prayogeṇa hitasya kim /
children.translated_text: What [use is] any endeavor for benefit if it involves harm?
Even protecting one's own body [is futile] when coupled with thirst for wealth. [46]
Just as the obtaining of the fruit of the <s>kiṃśuka</s> tree is useless to the hungry,
so the life of a wealthy person who does not give is purposeless. [47]

children.text: kāmāturāṇāṃ na bhayaṃ na lajjā kṣudhāturāṇāṃ na balaṃ na tejaḥ /
children.translated_text: For those afflicted by desire, there is neither fear nor shame; for those afflicted by hunger, neither strength nor vigor;

children.text: rogāturāṇāṃ na sukhaṃ na nidrā mārgāturāṇāṃ na bhayaṃ na vīryam // 48 //
children.translated_text: for those afflicted by disease, neither happiness nor sleep; for those afflicted by the journey, neither fear nor heroism. [48]

children.text: dhanalipsuḥ suhrit tyājyā bhāryā ca vyabhicāriṇī /
children.translated_text: A friend who covets wealth should be abandoned, as should an unfaithful wife,

children.text: adharmī ca nṛpaḥ krūro mantrī piśuna eva ca // 49 //
children.translated_text: an unrighteous and cruel king, and a minister who is a slanderer. [49]

children.text: kupradeśo hi durvyavasāyo duṣṭo 'tha vai suhṛt /
children.translated_text: An inauspicious place, a corrupt livelihood, and a wicked friend,

children.text: baidyo 'dakṣo 'pi duḥsevyam vastu heyā ime 'pi ca // 50 //
children.translated_text: an unskilled physician, and a thing difficult to employ — all these should be avoided. [50]
For one devoid of right conduct and understanding, excluded by many scriptural conventions, regarding the harmful as beneficial,
whose sole desire is merely to fill the belly — what is the difference between such a person and an animal? [51]
A pot half-filled with water is carried on the head with difficulty;
wicked people become angry indeed when served with honor and excessive attendance. [52]
By a little it rises high, by a little it goes down —

children.text: aho ! susadṛśī ceṣṭā tulāyaṣṭeḥ khalasya ca // 53 //
children.translated_text: Ah! How similar is the behavior of a balance-beam and a rogue! [53]

children.text: yathā bāryo na laśunasya gandhaḥ kastūrikācandanacandrasaṃjñaiḥ /
children.translated_text: Just as the smell of garlic cannot be removed by what are known as musk, sandalwood, and moonstone,

children.text: tathā na vāryā varaśāstraśikṣābhyāsena duṣṭasya ca duṣṭatāpi // 54 //
children.translated_text: so too the wickedness of the wicked cannot be removed by training in excellent scriptures. // 54 //
A wicked person should be avoided even if adorned with learning;

children.text: maṇinā bhūṣitaḥ sarpaḥ kimasau na bhayaṅkaraḥ // 55 //
children.translated_text: is a serpent decorated with a jewel any less terrifying? // 55 //
The wicked are of good disposition only so long as they are weak;

children.text: nyūne śaradi nīre hi nadīṃ sarve taranti ca // 56 //
children.translated_text: when the waters of autumn recede, everyone can cross the river. // 56 //
Just as excessive heat from fever and phlegm increase from dryness,
so the wicked are not transformed by virtuous conduct and good nature. // 57 //

children.text: duṣṭā narā bhṛtyagaṇo 'vamānī praśikṣitā naiva hayāḥ kubhāryā /
children.translated_text: Wicked men, disrespectful servants, untrained horses, and bad wives—

children.text: pratāḍanenaiva bhavanti namrāḥ sukarmayogyā na kadāpi caite // 58 //
children.translated_text: these become submissive only through punishment; they are never fit for good work. // 58 //

children.text: vṛthā vṛṣṭiḥ samudrasya vṛthā tṛptasya bhojanam /
children.translated_text: Rain is useless upon the ocean, food is useless to one who is sated,

children.text: vṛthā dānaṃ samarthasya vṛthā hīnasya satkṛtiḥ // 59 //
children.translated_text: a gift is useless to one who is wealthy, and honor is useless for the lowly. // 59 //

children.text: padmāni satputramukhe lasanti rohanti nūnaṃ kulaṭāsutasya /
children.translated_text: Lotuses shine on the face of a good son; but surely on the son of an unchaste woman

children.text: viṣasya patrāṇi yathā karoti duṣkarma yo vai labhate phalantat // 60 //
children.translated_text: grow leaves of poison—whoever does evil deeds, he reaps that fruit. // 60 //

children.text: abhracchāyā khale prītiḥ siddhamannaṃ ca yoṣitaḥ /
children.translated_text: The shadow of a cloud, the affection of a rogue, cooked food, and a woman,
a fire of straw, and a drop of frost—these six are like bubbles. // 61 //

children.text: śuṣkaṃ māṃsaṃ striyo vṛddhā madyaṃ ca taruṇaṃ dadhi /
children.translated_text: Dried meat, an aged woman, liquor, fresh yogurt,

children.text: nakte bhojo divā svāpaḥ ṣaḍete prāṇahāriṇaḥ // 62 //
children.translated_text: eating at night, and sleeping during the day—these six are destroyers of life. // 62 //
Fresh meat, fresh ghee, a young woman, rice cooked in milk,
warm water, and the shade of a tree—these six are life-giving. // 63 //

children.text: kāntāviyogaḥ svajanāpamāno ṛṇasya śeṣaḥ kunarasya sevā /
children.translated_text: Separation from a beloved, disrespect from one's own people, the remainder of a debt, serving a bad person,
and a friend who abandons one in poverty—these five burn without fire. // 64 //

children.text: karmī hyalābhī balino 'pakartā darpī ca bhikṣurhyadhanaḥ sukhārthī /
children.translated_text: An industrious person who gains nothing, a strong person who harms others, an arrogant beggar, a penniless seeker of pleasure,
and one who speaks harshly to beautiful beloveds—these five are people of false conduct. // 65 //
A giver of <s>dharma</s>, a giver of food, one who protects from fear, a teacher,
and a progenitor of one's body—these five are benefactors. // 66 //
One who has turned back from renunciation, a wife who looks at three husbands,
and a jackal freed from a trap—these three are considered deceivers. // 67 //
Cooks who are physicians, and kings who speak falsely,
and sinners of high lineage—these three persons are unworthy. // 68 //

children.text: yācakaḥ svādubhoji ca darpī bhikṣāparo bhavet /
children.translated_text: A beggar who is a gourmet, an arrogant one who lives on alms,
and an ignorant person who claims to be a scholar—these three invite ridicule. // 69 //

children.text: sakṛjjalpanti rājānaḥ āryo hi dṛśyate sakṛt /
children.translated_text: Kings speak but once, a noble person appears but once,
daughters are given but once—these three things happen only once. // 70 //
A corpulent ascetic, a hero who bears no wounds,
and a woman who sleeps alone—one should not trust these three. // 71 //
A <s>brāhmaṇa</s> who harms others, a king of unrighteous conduct,
and a monk who delights in sensual pleasures—these three on earth deserve blame. // 72 //
A learned person endowed with humility, a warrior who is exceedingly peaceful,
and a wealthy person who undertakes generosity—these three too are praiseworthy. // 73 //
A compassionate person absorbed in helping others, and a wicked person bent on destroying others,
and a child full of desires—these three on earth are indeed insatiable. // 74 //
Loss of wealth, mental anguish, a woman of bad conduct in the home,
deception, and dishonor—a wise person should not reveal these. // 75 //
The path of the moon and stars is known, the path of the sky is known by astronomers through calculation,

children.text: na dṛśyate tena gṛhe tu patnyāḥ kāmādimithyācaraṇaṃ kukṛtam // 76 //
children.translated_text: but the sinful misconduct of a wife's lust and the like at home cannot be seen by that means. // 76 //
What use is <s>Garuḍa</s> to one who knows the truth? What use is a physician to one who is healthy?

children.text: pāre gatasya kiṃ nāvā kāntayā kiṃ virāgiṇaḥ // 77 //
children.translated_text: What use is a boat to one who has reached the far shore? What use is a wife to one who is free from desire? // 77 //
In truth, the delight of gods, good people, and <s>brāhmaṇas</s> lies in the assembly of the learned;

children.text: gūḍhe vacasi bhojye 'sti prīti pṛthagjanasya ca // 78 //
children.translated_text: the delight of common people lies in secret talk and in food. // 78 //

children.text: śaile śaile na māṇikyaṃ mīne mīne na mauktim /
children.translated_text: Not every mountain has rubies, not every fish has a pearl,

children.text: sādhavo he na sarvatra candanaṃ na vane vane // 79 //
children.translated_text: good people are not found everywhere, nor is sandalwood in every forest. // 79 //

children.text: haṃso na bhāti caturo bakayūthamadhye gomāyumaṇḍalagato na vibhāti siṃhaḥ /
children.translated_text: A swan does not shine amidst a clever flock of herons; a lion placed amidst a pack of jackals does not shine;

children.text: jātyo na bhāti turagaḥ kharayūthamadhye vidvān na bhāti puruṣeṣu nirakṣareṣu // 80 //
children.translated_text: a noble horse does not shine amidst a herd of donkeys; a learned person does not shine among illiterate men. // 80 //
Voice is the beauty of cuckoos, modesty is the beauty of women,
learning is the beauty of the wise, and forbearance is the beauty of ascetics. // 81 //
What is forbearance in a powerful man who does not retaliate?

children.text: vinītāya ca śāntāya janāya kā sahiṣṇutā // 82 //
children.translated_text: And what is endurance in a person who is already humble and peaceful? // 82 //
Even a stranger who is helpful is a kinsman; even a kinsman who is harmful is a stranger.
A disease born in the body is harmful; a medicine from the forest is beneficial. // 83 //
The company of great people—whose elevation does it not bring about?
By association with a garland of flowers, even a thread is worn on the head. // 84 //
Where is the cleverness in deceiving those who have placed their trust?

children.text: aṅkamāruhya suptasya hantuḥ kiṃ nāma pauruṣam // 85 //
children.translated_text: What manliness is there in killing one who has climbed into one's lap and fallen asleep? // 85 //

children.text: kaumāre pitarau pātaḥ bhartrī rakṣati yauvane /
children.translated_text: In childhood, parents protect; in youth, the husband protects;
in old age, sons protect—a woman never deserves independence. // 86 //

children.text: āsaktirna bhaveddyāvat tāvattu guṇa eva saḥ /
children.translated_text: So long as attachment does not arise, that very quality remains a virtue;
but once great attachment enters, how can there be any acquisition of virtue? // 87 //
People generally judge others by their own ways;
sages, seeing a ghost, call him an ascetic. // 88 //
For men whose minds have been corrupted by wicked people, there is no trust even in good people;

children.text: bālaḥ payasā dagdho dadhyapi phūtkṛtya bhakṣayati // 89 //
children.translated_text: a child scalded by milk blows even on buttermilk before eating it. // 89 //
Like the pots of a water-wheel, a woman comes under control;
whoever undertakes the effort—indeed he succeeds, and that is wonderful. // 90 //
One who is honored by the great, the lowly considers as worthless as straw;
a crow perches on a <s>stūpa</s> worshipped by the wise. // 91 //
Though the fruit of the <s>ketaka</s> (screw-pine) tree indeed purifies water,
the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name. // 92 //

children.text: śiṣṭā na gṛhṇanti purā pratijñāṃ gṛhṇanti cet te kaṭhinapratijñām /
children.translated_text: The virtuous do not readily make promises; but if they do, they make firm promises;

children.text: aṅgikṛtāṃ tāṃ paripālayanti pāṣāṇarekhāmiva te tadānīm // 93 //
children.translated_text: they uphold what they have accepted, like an inscription carved in stone. // 93 //

children.text: prāpnoti vittaṃ hyadhamo ti kiñcid garvī pareṣāmavamānanāyām /
children.translated_text: When a low person obtains some wealth, he becomes arrogant in disrespecting others;

children.text: saṃjāyate labdhadhanaḥ sumartyaḥ supakvadhānyena samaṃ vinamraḥ // 94 //
children.translated_text: but a good person who has gained wealth becomes humble, like grain when it is ripe. // 94 //
There is no eye equal to wisdom, there is no darkness equal to delusion,
there is no enemy equal to disease, there is no fear equal to death. // 95 //
Therefore, cruel and unrelenting death is surely to be expected;
turning the mind away from desire, one should aspire to the true <s>dharma</s>. // 96 //

children.text: guṇā guṇajñeṣu guṇā bhavanti te nirguṇaṃ prāpya bhavanti doṣāḥ /
children.translated_text: Virtues are virtues among those who appreciate virtues; reaching one without virtues, they become faults;

children.text: susvādu toyāḥ prabhavanti nadyaḥ samudramāsādya bhavantyapeyāḥ // 97 //
children.translated_text: rivers flow with sweet water at their source, but reaching the ocean, they become undrinkable. // 97 //
Action whose consequences have been considered, performed by the intelligent,
will not meet with misfortune; and even if misfortune arises, it is averted. // 98 //

children.text: alpā dṛḍhā ye mṛdubhāṣiṇaśca tebhyo 'vadhānaṃ karaṇīyameva /
children.translated_text: Those who are small, firm, and soft-spoken—attention must indeed be paid to them;

children.text: niryāti sūryaḥ saghanāddhi meghāt syāt tatprakāśastu tadātitīkṣṇaḥ // 99 //
children.translated_text: for the sun emerges from a dense cloud, and its light then is exceedingly fierce. // 99 //

children.text: śāntipriyāḥ syuḥ khalu yauvane 'pi vaiduṣya evaṃ vinatā bhaveyuḥ /
children.translated_text: Those who love peace even in youth, who are humble in their learning,
who are patient and deeply modest in their brilliance—such conquerors of enemies are very rare. // 100 //
Among barbarians too there may be the prosperous, and among animals too the heroic,
but speakers of meaningful words who are truly virtuous are very rare indeed. // 101 //
Prosperity is fleeting, youth is perishable, and lives exist between the teeth of <s>Yama</s> (Death);

children.text: upekṣate tatra sukhaṃ na ceha janaḥ prapātastha ivāsti cāndhaḥ // 102 //
children.translated_text: yet one who does not heed this happiness here is like a blind person standing at the edge of a precipice. // 102 //

children.text: ye kleśarogiṇo bhuktvā na ca saddharmabheṣajam /
children.translated_text: Those who, afflicted by the disease of passions, do not take the medicine of the true <s>dharma</s>,

children.text: pramattā viṣayāsaktā bhavābdhiṃ na taranti te // 103 //
children.translated_text: heedless and attached to sense-objects, do not cross the ocean of existence. // 103 //
For a world whose nature is to keep moving, Death is seen standing overhead;
if even food becomes unpleasant at that point, what to speak of other activities? // 104 //
Death does not wait for the completion or non-completion of one's tasks;

children.text: śvastanaṃ cādya kuryācca pūrva madhyāhnikaṃ varam // 105 //
children.translated_text: one should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's work in the morning—that is best. // 105 //
Life in this world is unstable, youth is unstable, wealth is unstable;
wife and sons are unstable—only <s>dharma</s>, truth, and beneficence are enduring. // 106 //
A long life is fitting for a king; for a sage, a swift death is preferable;

children.text: sato jīvanamanto vā varaṃ tvākheṭakasya na // 107 //
children.translated_text: for a virtuous person, life or death is fine—but not so for a hunter. // 107 //

body.translated_text: The <s>Śatagāthā</s> (Hundred Verses) composed by master <s>Vararuci</s> is complete.

body.text: gātheyaṃ bhāratīyopādhyāyavinayacandreṇa bhoṭadeśīya lokacakṣu bhikṣuṇā dharmaprajñenānūditā nirṇītāceti /
body.translated_text: These verses were translated and edited by the Indian teacher <s>Vinayacandra</s> and the Tibetan monk <s>Dharmaprajña</s>, called <s>Lokacakṣu</s> (Eye of the World).
